name: Take Ivy

lead: Take Ivy is a photography book, first published in Japan in 1965, that documents how students at American Ivy League campuses dressed: oxford button-down shirts, khakis, tweed jackets, madras, loafers and rep ties.

For someone improving their appearance it works as a lookbook. The photographs show the proportions, layering and casual-but-neat mood of the Ivy look in candid campus settings, and the book is often cited by menswear writers and brands as a reference for preppy and 'old money' style.

paras: Readers use it for outfit reference: building a wardrobe around a small set of staples such as button-down shirts, chinos, blazers, knitwear and loafers, and copying the way pieces are combined. A reissued English edition has been available since 2010.

It is a book with no physical risks. Original 1965 copies are scarce in the West and have sold for high prices at auction, and the fashions pictured reflect one mid-century campus culture rather than every body type or setting.

lead: Take Ivy is a fashion photography book first published in Japan in 1965 by Fujingahosha. It collects candid photographs of students at Ivy League campuses in the United States and is widely treated as a primary document of the Ivy style, the button-down, chino and tweed look that later evolved into preppy dress.[1][2]

The book was written and photographed by four Japanese style enthusiasts: Teruyoshi Hayashida, Shosuke Ishizu, Toshiyuki Kurosu and Hajime (Paul) Hasegawa. Its title plays on Dave Brubeck's 1959 hit 'Take Five'.[1][2] Its images show young men in American-made clothing studying, cycling and lounging, which is why style communities use it as a visual guide to the look.[1]

Original copies are scarce in the West; powerHouse Books issued a new edition in 2010.[1] The New York Times described it as a treasure for fashion insiders, and brands such as Ralph Lauren and J. Crew have displayed copies in their stores.[1]

paras: Ivy style developed on elite American campuses from the 1920s to 1940s and was mainstream middle-class fashion from the late 1950s to the mid-1960s. Its characteristic pieces include sack-cut jackets, oxford cloth button-down shirts, chinos, penny loafers and knitwear.[3] Brooks Brothers and J. Press were major sellers, and by one account about 70 percent of suits sold in 1957 and 1958 were Ivy cut.[3]
Japan had its own Ivy boom in the early 1960s, driven by youth culture and brands such as VAN Jacket, whose designer Kensuke (Shosuke) Ishizu commissioned the project.[2]

In spring 1965 VAN Jacket sent photographer Hayashida and companions on roughly a month-long trip to eight campuses including Harvard, Yale, Princeton and Dartmouth, according to one account.[2] Hasegawa was the only fluent English speaker, and the team shot discreetly to capture students naturally.[2]

The book is reported to have sold more than 50,000 copies worldwide, and originals have fetched up to about $2,000 at auction.[1] It became a key reference for Japanese baby boomers and helped inspire the mid-2010s 'neo-Ivy' trend.[1] Ivy style itself resurfaced in the 2020s as the 'old money aesthetic'.[3]
